body:
Environmental effects of coal combustion

Coal-based electricity provides large quantities of power, but mining, transportation and combustion have environmental consequences. The substances released depend on the coal's composition, combustion conditions and installed pollution-control systems.

Pollutant or residueHow it arisesMain concern
Carbon dioxideOxidation of carbon in coalContribution to climate change
Sulphur dioxideCombustion of sulphur-containing materialAir pollution and acid deposition
Nitrogen oxidesHigh-temperature combustion reactionsAir pollution and formation of secondary pollutants
Particulate matterFly ash and other particles carried in flue gasRespiratory and environmental harm
Bottom ash and fly ashNon-combustible mineral matter remaining after burningSolid-waste handling and contamination risks

Coal mining can also disturb land, affect water quality and release methane. The severity of these effects varies with geological conditions, the type of mine and the safeguards used.

Fly ash, bottom ash and their uses

Fly ash consists of fine particles carried with the hot gases produced by coal combustion. Bottom ash is the heavier material that collects near the bottom of the furnace. The two are classified by where they are collected, not simply by their chemical composition.

Fly ash may be used in cement, concrete, bricks, blocks and other approved applications when it meets the required quality and environmental conditions. The use of ash can reduce the amount requiring disposal, but safe handling is still necessary. Ash ponds and other storage facilities must be managed to prevent dust dispersion, water contamination and structural failures.

Measures used to control pollution

  • Electrostatic precipitators and bag filters: remove particulate matter from flue gases.
  • Flue-gas desulphurisation: reduces sulphur dioxide emissions, commonly by using an absorbent such as limestone.
  • Low-NOx combustion measures and other treatment systems: limit nitrogen-oxide formation or remove nitrogen oxides from gases.
  • Coal washing: reduces some mineral impurities before combustion, though it generates rejects.
  • Ash utilisation and safe disposal: reduce the environmental burden of solid residues.
  • Improved thermal efficiency: lowers fuel consumption per unit of electricity and generally reduces emissions per unit generated.

An electrostatic precipitator removes particles, not the carbon dioxide produced by burning coal. Flue-gas desulphurisation primarily addresses sulphur dioxide. Neither should be described as a complete method of eliminating greenhouse-gas emissions.

Coal production and changing demand

India's Ministry of Coal reported domestic coal production of 1,047.52 million tonnes in FY 2024–25 and 1,040.08 million tonnes in FY 2025–26. These figures were published in a government release dated 2 August 2026. Both financial years exceeded 1 billion tonnes, but production in 2025–26 was slightly below the previous year's figure.

This distinction matters when interpreting trends: long-term expansion does not mean that every consecutive year's production must increase. Coal production, coal imports, coal stocks and electricity generated from coal are also separate statistical measures.

Why thermal power remains important during transition

Coal-fired stations can provide electricity when variable renewable output is insufficient, subject to fuel availability and plant operating constraints. They also support industrial electricity demand. However, coal combustion produces substantial carbon dioxide and other pollutants, so reducing the environmental impact of electricity generation is an important part of energy transition.

Energy transition is the gradual change in the fuels, technologies and infrastructure used to supply energy. Measures relevant to India's coal sector include more efficient thermal generation, lower-carbon electricity sources, energy conservation, improved electricity networks and suitable energy storage.

Solar and wind generation depend on weather and time of day. Balancing their output may require storage, flexible generation, stronger transmission networks and changes in electricity demand. Expanding renewable installed capacity alone does not prove that coal generation has already ceased to be necessary.

The objective is to improve energy security and reduce environmental damage while maintaining reliable and affordable energy. A well-designed transition therefore considers both the amount of clean energy installed and the amount of dependable energy actually delivered.

Prelims focus

  • Carbon dioxide is produced when carbon in coal burns.
  • Electrostatic precipitators control particulate emissions.
  • Flue-gas desulphurisation reduces sulphur dioxide emissions.
  • Fly ash is carried with flue gases; bottom ash accumulates in the lower furnace region.
  • India produced 1,040.08 million tonnes of coal in FY 2025–26, according to the Ministry of Coal release of 2 August 2026.
  • Trap: Removing fly ash does not remove the carbon dioxide formed by combustion.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 6, Combustion and Flame; NCERT, Contemporary India II, Class 10 Geography, chapter 5, Minerals and Energy Resources, section Conservation of Energy Resources; Central Electricity Authority, Ash Generation and Utilization at Coal/Lignite-Based Grid-Connected Thermal Power Stations for the Year 2024–25, report issued 23 March 2026; Ministry of Coal, Commercial Coal Mining: Fuelling India's Journey Towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Press Information Bureau release, 2 August 2026; consulted 15 November 2026.]

title: Coal Power: Emissions, Ash Management and Energy Transition

body:
What petroleum is

Petroleum is a naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons found in suitable geological formations. Crude petroleum is mainly liquid, while natural gas is mainly gaseous. Their compositions vary by reservoir. Crude oil cannot ordinarily be used directly as petrol or diesel; it must first undergo refining.

Petroleum is often called black gold because it is commercially valuable and yields many useful fuels and chemical raw materials. This expression does not mean that every petroleum deposit is black or that petroleum is a metallic mineral.

Formation and accumulation of oil and gas

Oil and natural gas commonly originate from organic matter deposited with sediment, particularly microscopic organisms in ancient aquatic environments. With burial over geological time, increasing temperature and pressure transform suitable organic material into hydrocarbons.

The rock in which petroleum originates is called the source rock. Oil and gas may move from this rock into another formation containing connected pores or fractures. Such a formation is called a reservoir rock. Petroleum can accumulate where a suitable geological structure and an impermeable sealing rock prevent further migration.

In a simplified petroleum trap, natural gas may occupy the upper part of the reservoir, oil may lie below it and water may occupy the lower part because of differences in density. Real reservoirs may have more complex fluid distributions.

Oil is generally stored in pore spaces and fractures within reservoir rocks, not in a vast underground open lake. The presence of sedimentary rock alone does not guarantee a commercially productive petroleum deposit.

Exploration and production

Exploration identifies geological formations that may contain hydrocarbons. Geological mapping and seismic surveys help investigators understand the arrangement of underground rock layers. Seismic methods use reflected waves to infer subsurface structures.

An exploratory well is drilled to test whether hydrocarbons are present in economically useful quantities. If a discovery is suitable for development, production wells and associated equipment are established. Wells may be located onshore, on land, or offshore, beneath the sea.

Oil may rise through a well due to reservoir pressure or may need pumping or other production assistance. The extracted mixture is separated and treated before oil and gas enter transport and processing systems.

India's sedimentary basins

India has 26 sedimentary basins in the classification used by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons. However, a sedimentary basin is a geological area of potential interest; it is not necessarily a commercially producing oilfield.

Oil or gas regionLocationImportant association
Assam ShelfAssamDigboi, Naharkatiya and Moran
Cambay BasinGujaratAnkleshwar, Kalol and Mehsana
Mumbai HighOffshore Maharashtra, Arabian SeaMajor offshore petroleum-producing region
Rajasthan BasinRajasthanImportant onshore oil production, including the Barmer region
Krishna-Godavari BasinEastern offshore and adjoining land areasOil and natural gas resources
Cauvery BasinSoutheastern IndiaHydrocarbon exploration and production

Gujarat's petroleum resources

The Cambay Basin is central to Gujarat's petroleum geography. Important fields include Ankleshwar, Kalol and Mehsana. Other names associated with petroleum resources in older geographical accounts include Nawagam and Lunej. Petroleum resources in Gujarat are linked to the state's refining, pipeline and petrochemical industries.

Gujarat's onshore Cambay oilfields should be distinguished from Mumbai High, which is an offshore field in the Arabian Sea off Maharashtra. The Krishna-Godavari Basin is associated with India's eastern coast, not the Gulf of Khambhat.

Important historical developments

Digboi in Assam is an important early petroleum-producing centre. The national oil-exploration programme expanded significantly following the establishment of the Oil and Natural Gas Commission in 1956. Mumbai High was discovered in 1974, and production commenced in 1976.

Discovering a resource, estimating the amount present and producing it commercially are separate stages. An increase in estimated geological resources does not automatically mean that production has increased.

Prelims focus

  • Petroleum commonly accumulates in porous reservoir rock beneath an impermeable seal.
  • Seismic surveys help identify subsurface geological structures.
  • Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran are associated with Assam.
  • Ankleshwar, Kalol and Mehsana are associated with Gujarat's Cambay Basin.
  • Mumbai High was discovered in 1974; production began in 1976.
  • Trap: A sedimentary basin is not necessarily a commercially producing oilfield.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 5, Coal and Petroleum, printed pp. 59–61; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, section Petroleum, printed pp. 79–80; Directorate General of Hydrocarbons, Introduction to Indian Oil and Gas Sector and Statutory Clearances, chapter 1, section 1.2, Sedimentary Basins of India, dghindia.gov.in; consulted 15 November 2026.]

body:
Why crude petroleum must be refined

Crude petroleum contains a mixture of hydrocarbons with different molecular sizes and boiling characteristics. It must be separated and processed to obtain fuels and other useful products. This industrial process is called petroleum refining.

The first major separation stage in many refineries is fractional distillation. Crude oil is heated, and its components separate into fractions according to their boiling ranges. Lighter fractions are collected from cooler upper regions of a fractionating column, while heavier fractions are collected from lower regions.

Important refinery products

Product or fractionTypical application
LPGCooking and industrial fuel
NaphthaPetrochemical feedstock and further processing
Petrol or gasolineFuel for spark-ignition road vehicles
Kerosene and aviation turbine fuelHeating, lighting and aviation applications
DieselHeavy vehicles, machinery and generators
Lubricating oilReduction of friction in machinery
Paraffin waxCandles and other manufactured products
BitumenRoad construction and waterproofing

These products are commonly associated with different boiling ranges, but modern refineries do more than separate existing fractions. Processes such as cracking break heavier hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones, while other processing steps improve fuel quality and remove unwanted substances such as sulphur.

Petrochemicals and non-fuel uses

Petroleum and natural gas are also raw materials for petrochemicals. These are used to manufacture plastics, synthetic fibres, detergents, solvents and many other industrial products. Using a petroleum-derived substance as a chemical feedstock is different from burning petroleum as a fuel.

For example, naphtha can provide raw materials for chemical manufacturing, while diesel is commonly burned in engines. Both may originate from crude oil, but their immediate industrial purposes differ.

Location of refineries

Refineries may be located close to oil-producing regions, ports or large markets. A field-based refinery is associated with the source of crude oil, while a market-based refinery is located to serve important consumption and industrial centres. Transport infrastructure can reduce the need for a refinery to stand directly above an oilfield.

Digboi in Assam is a standard example of a field-based refinery. Barauni in Bihar is used in geographical textbooks as a market-based example. Coastal refineries can receive imported crude by tanker and distribute products to inland markets.

Major refinery locations in Gujarat

Gujarat is a major refining and petrochemical centre because it combines petroleum resources, ports, industrial demand and transport infrastructure.

  • Gujarat Refinery, Koyali: operated by Indian Oil Corporation near Vadodara. It began operating in 1965 and is linked to petroleum-product pipeline networks.
  • Jamnagar refinery complex: operated by Reliance Industries and associated with large-scale petroleum refining and petrochemicals.
  • Vadinar refinery: operated by Nayara Energy near the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat, with marine facilities for crude handling and product movement.

Koyali is a refinery location, not an oilfield name. Similarly, Jamnagar and Vadinar identify refinery centres; their refining activity does not prove that all crude processed there was produced locally.

Crude oil, petroleum products and India's trade

A country may import large quantities of crude oil and still possess extensive refining capacity. Some refined products may be supplied to domestic markets, while others may be exported. Therefore, high refining capacity does not establish crude-oil self-sufficiency.

The petroleum chain contains distinct activities: crude exploration and production, import and transport, refining, product storage, distribution and final consumption. Disruption at one stage can affect later stages even if refinery machinery remains operational.

Prelims focus

  • Fractional distillation separates crude-oil components by boiling range.
  • Cracking converts heavier hydrocarbons into smaller molecules.
  • Naphtha is an important petrochemical feedstock.
  • Bitumen is associated with road surfacing.
  • Koyali is near Vadodara; Jamnagar and Vadinar are also major Gujarat refinery centres.
  • Trap: A refinery's location does not necessarily indicate the origin of the crude oil it processes.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 5, Coal and Petroleum, section 5.2, Refining of Petroleum, printed pp. 59–60; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, section Petroleum, printed p. 80; Indian Oil Corporation, Gujarat Refinery, iocl.com/gujarat-refinery; Reliance Industries, Refining and Marketing, Jamnagar Refineries, ril.com; Nayara Energy, Vadinar Refinery, nayaraenergy.com; consulted 15 November 2026.]
